title: SAML and Kerberos: what each needs to work

prose.text: Authentication method decides how a request gets an identity; whether it is demanded at all is [[zia.authentication.location-enforcement]].

prose.label: SAML.
prose.text: {{saml-sp}} {{saml-idp-reachability}} Org-level SAML switches (samlEnabled, autoProvision) are in [[zia.authentication.settings]].

prose.label: Kerberos.
prose.text: {{kerberos-no-cookie}} {{kerberos-explicit-only}} {{kerberos-clients}} {{kerberos-network}} The per-location Kerberos switch is in [[zia.authentication.location-enforcement]].

Hosted DB (form-based login with the service's own users) is the third method; its password fields are in [[zia.authentication.settings]]. Which method tenants favour is open {{gap:deployment-defaults}}.

checks.do: How the failing traffic is forwarded, PAC or tunnel, since Kerberos is supported only in explicit mode.
Whether the IdP host is exempted on that forwarding path.
Whether a Zscaler cookie was present on the request, since Kerberos challenges a request that has none.

saml-sp.statement: With SAML single sign-on the Zscaler service is the service provider, and SAML SSO is used for provisioning and authenticating users. Before configuring it, the SAML SSL certificate must be obtained from the IdP and the XML metadata exported from it.

quotes: You can configure the Zscaler service as the service provider (SP) and use Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) Single Sign-On (SSO) for provisioning and authenticating users.
Obtain the SAML SSL certificate from your identity provider (IdP).
Export the XML metadata from your IdP.

saml-idp-reachability.statement: The IdP must be reachable without a user identity. With PAC-file forwarding, the redirected IdP URL must be in the PAC file's authentication exemption list or authentication fails; with transparent forwarding, the SAML IdP traffic must be exempted from the GRE or IPSec tunnel, for example by a route at the gateway router that sends it directly to the internet.

quotes: If you are using PAC files to forward traffic to the Zscaler service, add the redirected URL to the authentication exemption list in the PAC files. Otherwise, the authentication fails.
the current user isn't yet authorized to use the service, so the request never passes through the Internet & SaaS (ZIA) Public Service Edge.

If you are transparently forwarding traffic to the Zscaler service, you must exempt the SAML IdP traffic from the GRE or IPSec tunnel. You can do this by adding a route at the gateway router to forward the traffic directly to the internet.

kerberos-no-cookie.statement: Kerberos does not use cookies; it is ticket-based. When the Public Service Edge finds no Zscaler cookie for the domain in the request, it issues a 407 Negotiate challenge, and the client answers with a ticket in the proxy authorization header.

quotes: Unlike the other supported authentication mechanisms, Kerberos doesn't use cookies for authentication.
It is a ticket-based authentication protocol
If the Public Service Edge doesn't find a Zscaler cookie for the domain in the HTTP request, it issues a 407 Negotiate challenge.
The client sends the HTTP request with the proxy authorization header and ticket, which contains the client information.

kerberos-explicit-only.statement: Kerberos is supported only for traffic forwarded in explicit mode (a PAC file points the browser at the service). It is not supported for transparent forwarding through a GRE or IPSec tunnel when the browser is not using a PAC file, and users must already be provisioned: Kerberos authenticates, it does not provision.

quotes: Use a PAC file to forward traffic to the Zscaler service.
The service supports Kerberos authentication only for traffic forwarded in explicit mode.
It doesn't support Kerberos for traffic forwarded in transparent mode, which is traffic forwarded through a GRE or IPSec tunnel and the browser isn't configured to use a PAC file to forward traffic.
Kerberos is an authentication mechanism. It is not a provisioning method
Users must be provisioned on the Zscaler service before they can use Kerberos for authentication.

kerberos-clients.statement: Kerberos lets the service authenticate applications that do not support cookies, such as Office 365 and Windows Metro apps, and apply user, group and department policy to FTP and to HTTPS without decrypting it. It is not supported on Windows XP, iOS or Android.

quotes: It enables the Zscaler service to authenticate users when they use applications that do not support cookies, such as Office 365 and Windows Metro apps.
The service can enforce granular user, group, and department policies on proxied FTP transactions as well as HTTPS transactions, without having to decrypt the HTTPS transactions.
The Zscaler service doesn't support Kerberos on Windows XP, Apple iOS, or Android devices.

kerberos-network.statement: Kerberos needs the site's DNS to resolve the Zscaler service host names and the firewall to allow ports 88/8800, and the domain suffix of the client or server in the ticket must be a registered domain in the Zscaler account.

quotes: Ensure that the DNS server on site can resolve the Zscaler service host names
Ensure that your firewall allows connections to port 88/8800 to enable Kerberos authentication.
Ensure that the domain suffix of either the client or server, in the Kerberos ticket obtained from your organization's domain controller, is a registered domain in the Zscaler account.

deployment-defaults.title: Which authentication methods tenants use in practice
deployment-defaults.detail: Unverified legacy statement: SAML and Kerberos are the production defaults for enterprise tenants, and Hosted DB is used mainly for guest Wi-Fi or contractor populations without SSO coverage. No registered source states this. Only a vendor deployment guide or tenant survey could state it; it is a usage claim, not product behavior.
deployment-defaults.blocks: recommending a method for a given population
